eligibility_reason: Three new-data studies (new Facebook and undergraduate samples) test whether the five-factor MUSIC music-preference structure reported in the separately published Rentfrow, Goldberg, & Levitin (2011, JPSP) replicates; Study 1 uses a subset of that paper's Study 2 excerpts, and Studies 2-3 test it within jazz and rock. The authors frame the paper as 'a replication and extension of the MUSIC model' (a self-replication).

effects.original_title: The structure of musical preferences: A five-factor model
effects.original_authors: Rentfrow, Peter J.; Goldberg, Lewis R.; Levitin, Daniel J.
effects.original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
effects.replication_study: Study 1 (mixed-genre excerpts, Facebook 'My Personality' sample, N = 1,057)
effects.outcome: Factor structure of liking ratings for 15 s audio excerpts (five MUSIC factors), plus the auditory/psychological attribute profiles that define each factor
effects.contrast: not applicable: factor-analytic structure; compared to the original's factors and to its Table 4 attribute correlations (column-vector correlations)
effects.description: Individual differences in liking for audio excerpts of real music from many genres are described by five orthogonal dimensions - Mellow, Unpretentious, Sophisticated, Intense, and Contemporary (MUSIC) - each defined by distinct auditory and psychological attributes.
effects.citation_sentence: Study 1 was designed to replicate the five-factor music-preference model reported in Rentfrow, Goldberg, and Levitin (2011) and to extend that work by investigating a larger set of auditory and psychological attributes.
effects.evidence: Study 1 Results/Summary: "The final five-factor solution was consistent with our expectations and clearly resembled the MUSIC model." ... "The results from the present study are consistent with previous research on the MUSIC model (Rentfrow, Goldberg, & Levitin, 2011)." Attribute profiles vs. original Table 4: "column-vector correlations = .96, .85, .92, .97, and .81, for M, U, S, I, and C".
effects.notes: Self-replication (Rentfrow, Goldberg and Levitin are co-authors here). Stimuli are a subset (50 pieces) of the original's Study 2 Getty Images excerpts; the population was deliberately changed ('a large and representative sample of Internet users, as opposed to music fans') and attributes were added, so close extension rather than direct (direct is a defensible alternative). The attribute-profile convergence (14 shared attributes) is coded as part of the same claim (it is how the factors are identified as MUSIC), not as a separate entry; a coder splitting 'factor structure' and 'attribute definitions' into two claims would get two success rows. original_url left blank: the paper's reference list gives no DOI.

effects.original_title: The structure of musical preferences: A five-factor model
effects.original_authors: Rentfrow, Peter J.; Goldberg, Lewis R.; Levitin, Daniel J.
effects.original_journal: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
effects.replication_study: Study 2 (jazz excerpts; Facebook sample N = 913 and University of Texas undergraduate sample N = 408)
effects.outcome: Factor structure of liking ratings for jazz-only excerpts (whether five MUSIC-like factors emerge) and convergence of their attribute profiles with the MUSIC factors
effects.contrast: not applicable: factor-analytic structure; jazz factors compared to the MUSIC factors via attribute column-vector correlations
effects.description: Individual differences in music preferences are described by five MUSIC dimensions (Mellow, Unpretentious, Sophisticated, Intense, Contemporary) defined by particular auditory and psychological attributes.
effects.citation_sentence: Studies 2 and 3 were designed to examine the structure of preferences for pieces of music within genres. Specifically, preferences for various jazz musical pieces were assessed in Study 2 and preferences for various rock pieces were assessed in Study 3. [General Discussion:] Using multiple pieces of music, methods, and samples, three studies were conducted to test the replicability of the five-dimensional music-preference model ... Taken together, these results provide almost complete replication of the MUSIC model
effects.evidence: Study 2 Results/Summary: "The five-factor solution that emerged in the Internet sample was highly consistent with our expectations and clearly resembled the MUSIC model." ... "The present results supported our hypothesis and revealed five jazz-preference factors." But: "at least four of the five jazz-preference factors clearly resemble the MUSIC factors"; Sophisticated psychological convergence = -.40 (Table 4).
effects.notes: Self-replication. The original did not test within-genre structure; this is an extension of the five-factor claim to a single genre with new (jazz) stimuli, so close extension (conceptual is a possible alternative). The citation sentence for this study does not itself name Rentfrow et al. (2011); the study's own text says 'if the MUSIC model is robust ... we should expect to find factors that resemble MUSIC'. Result: authors say their hypothesis was supported and five factors emerged, but the Sophisticated jazz factor 'showed no convergence on the psychological attributes' (r = -.40), so a second coder could call it inconclusive (partial). The Internet and undergraduate samples are treated as one entry: they are two samples of one study, the undergraduate sample is used as a reliability check of the same structure (congruence .96, .94, .97, .68, .94), and the attribute analysis pools them.

effects.contrast: not applicable: factor-analytic structure; rock factors compared to the MUSIC factors via attribute column-vector correlations
effects.description: Individual differences in music preferences are described by five MUSIC dimensions (Mellow, Unpretentious, Sophisticated, Intense, Contemporary) defined by particular auditory and psychological attributes.
effects.citation_sentence: Studies 2 and 3 were designed to examine the structure of preferences for pieces of music within genres. Specifically, preferences for various jazz musical pieces were assessed in Study 2 and preferences for various rock pieces were assessed in Study 3. [General Discussion:] Using multiple pieces of music, methods, and samples, three studies were conducted to test the replicability of the five-dimensional music-preference model ... effects.evidence: Study 3 Summary: "The results from this study once again support the hypothesis ... results from the factor analyses revealed five rock-preference factors ... those factors were defined by attributes that resembled the preference models observed in Studies 1 and 2." Rock vs mixed-genre psychological column-vector correlations = .93, .70, .91, .97, and .25 (M, U, S, I, C).
effects.notes: Self-replication; extension of the five-factor claim to rock-only stimuli, so close extension (conceptual possible). Authors call it support, but the Contemporary factor converged weakly with the mixed-genre factor on psychological attributes (.25) and convergence with the jazz factors was lower (S = -.53, C = -.19 psychological), and parallel analysis suggested six factors in the Internet sample; a second coder could call it inconclusive. Internet and undergraduate samples coded as one entry (congruence .86, .98, .92, .98, .85), as in Study 2. General Discussion: 28 of 35 attribute comparisons significantly similar; 'almost complete replication of the MUSIC model'.
